etymology: From the Hebrew 'emeq he-charuts, “the valley of decision,” the noun charuts springing from charats, to cut, sharpen, and so to determine; the margin reads “concision” or “threshing.” It is Joel’s name for the valley of Jehoshaphat, “the LORD judgeth.”
biblical_def: Joel lifts the eye of the church to a valley that no map can fix, the valley of decision, which is the valley of Jehoshaphat, where the LORD declares, “I will also gather all nations, and will bring them down…and will plead with them there” (Joe 3:2). It is the floor of the last assize. The prophet cries, “Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision” (Joe 3:14). The word rendered decision carries the sense of threshing, the sharp stroke that parts the wheat from the chaff, and so the valley is no place of man’s deliberation but of God’s determination. Here the Judge of all the earth does right. Before Him shall be gathered all nations, and He shall separate them one from another, “as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats” (Mat 25:32); the books are opened, and the dead are judged every man according to his works (Rev 20:12). This is a sober word, not a rumor to be softened. The valley of decision teaches that history bends toward a reckoning, that God’s long patience is not slumber, and that the day is near. Yet the elect need not fear the threshingfloor, for their names are written in the Lamb’s book of life, and the Shepherd who divides has already numbered His own. Flee, then, to Christ before the sickle falls.

corruption_summary: The age dismisses a coming day of judgment as myth or metaphor; the valley of decision recalls the church to the certainty of the great assize.
corruption_paragraphs: The great corruption of the present hour is the quiet deletion of the last judgment. Men will speak of a God of love while striking from their creed the day when He shall judge the world in righteousness, and the valley of decision is folded into figure, as though Joel spoke only of inward choices and not of the LORD gathering all nations to be judged. But the prophet is plain: the day of the LORD is near, and the threshing is real.

The recovery is a sober and unflinching eschatology. Scripture sets a day, and appoints a Judge, and opens the books; the dead, small and great, shall stand before God, and be judged according to their works (Rev 20:12), the sheep parted from the goats (Mat 25:32). This is no manufactured terror but the settled testimony of the word. Let the church preach it whole—wrath to come and refuge in Christ—that sinners may flee to the Shepherd before the sickle falls, and that the saints may lift up their heads, knowing their names are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

etymology: Hebrew 'emeq Sukkoth, “the valley of booths,” from sukkah, a booth or tabernacle, so named because Jacob built booths there for his cattle (Gen 33:17); a trans-Jordan valley the LORD claims as His to divide.
biblical_def: When the LORD would prove His right to the land, He did not argue; He apportioned it. “God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth” (Psa 60:6). Succoth lay beyond Jordan, in the trans-Jordan lowland where Jacob once built booths for his cattle; and David, singing of the LORD’s conquests, hears God claim that far valley as His own to measure with the line. To mete out is the act of an owner, not a suitor. The whole land—Shechem on this side, Succoth on that—is the LORD’s, and He portions it to whom He will. Here is the doctrine of sovereign inheritance writ in geography: the earth is the LORD’s, and every allotment among the tribes, from Heshbon and Mahanaim outward (Josh 13:26), came not by conquest merely but by grant. As the mountains stand round about Jerusalem, so the LORD stands round about His people (Psa 125:2), holding both land and heir in His hand. What comfort for the saint, whose inheritance is not seized but given, sure because the Giver is sovereign. Yet the trans-Jordan booths were never the rest itself; they pointed on, for here we have no continuing city, but seek one to come (Heb 13:14). The valley of Succoth teaches us to receive our portion from His hand and to look beyond it to the abiding city.
webster_summary: A trans-Jordan valley of booths that the LORD claims as His to portion—“I will…mete out the valley of Succoth” (Psa 60:6); a witness to God’s sovereign ownership of the land and the inheritance He grants.

The principle to recover is the sovereign ownership of God over all the earth, and His free right to portion the inheritance. etymology: Hebrew 'emeq ha-melek, “the king’s dale,” also called the valley of Shaveh; a level vale near Salem, from melek, king, and 'emeq, valley.
biblical_def: One dale, two monuments, and the whole vanity of the world laid bare between them. The king’s dale, the valley of Shaveh, was where the king of Sodom came out to meet Abram returning from the slaughter of the kings (Gen 14:17); and it was there that Abram refused the spoils of Sodom, that no man might say he had made him rich, and took instead the blessing of Melchizedek. In that same dale, generations later, Absalom “reared up for himself a pillar…for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance: and he called the pillar after his own name” (2Sa 18:18). Behold the contrast the ground itself preaches. Abram sought no memorial and gained an everlasting name; Absalom, grasping at remembrance, left only a heap called Absalom’s place, a rebel’s cenotaph over an empty pit. The one blessed of God needed no stone; the one at war with God could build nothing that would stand. So it is with every name reared apart from the LORD: “here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14), and the pillars of the proud crumble while the meek inherit. Lift up your eyes, rather, unto the hills, from whence cometh your help (Psa 121:1). The king’s dale bids us build no monument to self, but to hide our name in Christ, in whom alone it is kept in remembrance for ever.

etymology: Hebrew Libnah, “whiteness,” from laban, to be white, perhaps of white poplars or chalk; here a wilderness encampment between Rimmon-parez and Rissah, distinct from Libnah the walled town of Judah.
biblical_def: Between Rimmon-parez and Rissah, in the long roll of the wilderness marches, stands a single line: “they departed from Rimmonparez, and pitched in Libnah” (Num 33:20), and again, “they removed from Libnah, and pitched at Rissah” (Num 33:21). This Libnah is not the town of Judah that later sheltered priests, but a nameless camp in the middle of the wandering, a place remembered for nothing but that Israel tarried there and moved on. Yet the Holy Ghost thought it worth recording. The forty-two stations of Numbers thirty-three are a monument to a truth the pilgrim easily forgets: God keeps the account of every stage of the journey, not the mountaintops only but the dull middle, the camps where nothing seems to happen. Israel pitched and Israel removed at the word of the LORD, and each obscure remove was ordered by the pillar of cloud. So the Christian’s path is numbered station by station by a faithful hand; the years that leave no story are not lost years, for He that led them through the great and terrible wilderness led them by Libnah too. We are strangers and pilgrims here (1Pe 2:11), and the God who wrote down Libnah writes down our forgotten days. Take heart, wayfarer, in the unremarkable stretch: the middle of the march is watched as surely as the exodus and the entrance, and not one encampment falls outside His covenant care.
webster_summary: A wilderness encampment between Rimmon-parez and Rissah in Israel’s wandering (Num 33:20-21), distinct from Libnah the town of Judah; a witness to God’s faithful care over the nameless middle of the pilgrimage.

etymology: Hebrew Sela' ha-machlekoth, “the rock of divisions” or “of escapes,” from sela', a rock or crag, and chalaq, to divide, part; so named where Saul was divided from David.
biblical_def: David was all but taken. Saul had compassed him and his men about in the wilderness of Maon, closing upon them as the Ziphites betrayed his hiding in the hill of Hachilah (1Sa 23:19); the net was drawn, and flesh had no escape. Then heaven moved a messenger: word came that the Philistines had invaded the land, and “Saul returned from pursuing after David…therefore they called that place Selahammahlekoth” (1Sa 23:28), the rock of divisions, the crag that split the hunter from the hunted at the last instant. Not David’s sword nor his cunning delivered him, but a providence timed to the breath. The LORD who numbers the hairs governs also the marches of Philistines and the fears of kings, and He bent them all to divide Saul from His anointed. Here is refuge for the pressed believer: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble (Psa 46:1), and His help arrives not a moment early nor a moment late. When thou passest through the waters, He is with thee (Isa 43:2), and He will interpose a whole invasion sooner than let His own be swallowed. The rock of divisions stands for every providential interruption by which the Father parts His children from the jaws that gape for them. What men call coincidence, faith calls the finger of God, dividing the pursuer from the pursued and setting the ransomed free.
webster_summary: “The rock of divisions,” where Saul turned from pursuing David to meet the Philistines and David escaped (1Sa 23:28); a witness to the providential interruption that divides the pursuer from the pursued.

etymology: Hebrew 'Allon bakuth, “the oak of weeping,” from 'allon, an oak or great tree, and bakah, to weep; the tree beneath Bethel where Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, was buried.
biblical_def: Even the tears of a servant are named and remembered in the book of God. Beneath Bethel, under an oak, they buried Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, “and the name of it was called Allonbachuth” (Gen 35:8), the oak of weeping. She was no princess, no prophet—a nurse, an old woman who had carried Rebekah from Padan-aram—yet her death drew the household of Jacob to honest grief, and the place kept the memory of their weeping. Scripture does not despise the sorrow of the saints nor hurry them past the grave with a hollow cheer. It sanctifies their tears, giving the very tree a name that means weeping. Yet the oak of weeping stands hard by Bethel, the house of God, where Jacob had seen the ladder set up to heaven; and so the grief is hedged about with covenant. Those who pass through the valley of Baca, the vale of weeping, make it a well (Psa 84:6), for godly sorrow springs into hope. The LORD leads His mourners beside the still waters (Psa 23:2) and renews the strength of them that wait upon Him, that they may mount up with wings as eagles (Isa 40:31). Allon-bachuth teaches us to weep without despair. We sorrow, but not as others which have no hope; the dust of the faithful, like Deborah’s, rests under the shadow of the house of God, awaiting the morning when death itself shall be swallowed up in victory.

etymology: Hebrew 'Abel Mitsrayim, “the mourning of the Egyptians,” a play on 'abel, mourning, and 'abel, a meadow, with Mitsrayim, Egypt; named at the threshingfloor of Atad beyond Jordan.
biblical_def: When Jacob died, the mourning was so great that even Egypt wept, and a heathen land gave its name to the grief. At the threshingfloor of Atad, beyond Jordan, Joseph and the elders of Pharaoh’s house made a mourning of seven days, until the Canaanites said, “This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians: wherefore the name of it was called Abelmizraim” (Gen 50:11), the mourning of the Egyptians. Consider the honor God set upon the death of His saint. A shepherd, a pilgrim, a man who confessed himself a stranger, was carried up out of Egypt with chariots and horsemen, and the nations paused to mourn a patriarch. But the deeper honor lay in this: Jacob would not be buried in the wealth of Egypt but borne over Jordan to the cave of Machpelah, into the land of promise, that his very grave might preach his faith. He desired a better country, that is, an heavenly (Heb 11:16), and his burial in Canaan was a confession that the promise held beyond death. So the saints are strangers and pilgrims still (1Pe 2:11), seeking a continuing city not here but to come (Heb 13:14). Abel-mizraim teaches that the death of the righteous is precious in the LORD’s sight, weighty enough to move the nations, and that where a believer chooses to be laid may itself be a sermon of hope in the resurrection of the just.

etymology: Hebrew Qiryath chutsoth, “city of streets,” from qiryah, a city, and chuts, a street or outside place; Balak’s town whither he brought Balaam to curse Israel.
biblical_def: Balak thought a city of streets and a hired tongue could undo the blessing of the Almighty. “And Balaam went with Balak, and they came unto Kirjathhuzoth” (Num 22:39), the city of streets, whither the king of Moab brought the soothsayer to curse Israel encamped below. Sacrifices were offered on the high places, silver was promised, and every art of enchantment was brought to bear—and it came to nothing, for no divination avails against Jacob. God had blessed, and Balaam could not reverse it; the mouth hired to curse was made to bless four times over. Here the schemes of kings dash themselves upon the naked sovereignty of God. As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people (Psa 125:2), a wall no purchased prophet can breach; He is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble (Psa 46:1). Though Balak paved his streets with altars, the word of the LORD overruled every one, for when God says “I will be with thee” (Isa 43:2), no tempest of malice shall overflow His own. Kirjath-huzoth stands for every council chamber and every marketplace where the enemies of the church plot her ruin with money and words. Let the streets of Moab be full of curses; the blessing of God is surer than them all, and they that are blessed of Him abide blessed, though all the Balaks of the earth conspire.

corruption_summary: Kirjath-huzoth recovers the futility of every scheme to curse the people whom God has blessed, and the word of the LORD overruling the plots of kings.
corruption_paragraphs: Kirjath-huzoth, the city of streets, was where Balak spent his silver and his sacrifices to buy a curse, and got a blessing. Every art of enchantment was brought to bear against Israel, and it came to nothing, for God had blessed, and no divination avails against Jacob. The schemes of the king dashed themselves upon the naked sovereignty of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A town of Moab stirs no modern quarrel. The principle to recover is that no council chamber and no purchased tongue can reverse the blessing of God upon His church. As the mountains stand round about Jerusalem, so the LORD stands round about His people; they that are blessed of Him abide blessed, though all the Balaks of the earth conspire.

etymology: Hebrew Minnith, of uncertain root, perhaps from manah, to apportion or count, and so “distribution” or “allotted portion”; a city of Ammon, later noted for its wheat.
biblical_def: The son of a harlot, thrust out by his brethren, became the rod by which the LORD broke Ammon. Jephthah, whom Gilead had despised, “smote them from Aroer, even till thou come to Minnith, even twenty cities…with a very great slaughter” (Jdg 11:33), and Ammon was subdued before Israel. Minnith marks the far reach of that deliverance, the boundary to which God carried the victory through a most unlikely judge. It is His constant way to save by the weak, that the excellency of the power might be of Him: by Gideon and his three hundred beside the well of Harod (Jdg 7:1), by a shepherd boy, by a carpenter’s reputed son. Minnith was known also in later days for its wheat, traded even to the merchants of Tyre—a fruitful land, for the LORD who gives the victory gives also the increase, opening rivers in high places and making the wilderness a pool of water (Isa 41:18), turning dry ground into watersprings (Psa 107:35). So the field won by the sword became a field of harvest. Minnith teaches the church to despise no instrument God chooses and to expect fruitfulness where He has given the land. The Judge who raised up Jephthah still overthrows the proud by the lowly, and the ground His people inherit He crowns with bread. Let none boast in his own strength; the slaughter and the wheat alike are of the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew Sela' 'Etam, “the rock of Etam,” 'Etam meaning “place of ravenous creatures” or “lair,” and sela', a cleft rock or crag; Samson’s stronghold in Judah.
biblical_def: After Samson smote the Philistines hip and thigh with a great slaughter, “he went down and dwelt in the top of the rock Etam” (Jdg 15:8), the cleft crag whither the enemy dared not follow. Thither three thousand men of Judah went down to fetch him, fearful of their masters (Jdg 15:11), and bound their own deliverer to hand him over. The rock was Samson’s refuge, a high stronghold in the day of his strength; yet the deliverer of Israel was himself a flawed and divided man, and the rock could shelter his body but not mend his soul. Here the type strains toward its fulfilment. Samson hid in a rock, but he was not the Rock; he saved with one hand and fell by his own lusts with the other. He points beyond himself to a greater Deliverer, the spiritual Rock that followed Israel, and that Rock was Christ (1Co 10:4), a hiding place from the wind, a covert from the tempest, the shadow of a great rock in a weary land (Isa 32:2). In Him the people are hid indeed, not for a season but for ever, and He needs no cleft to shelter Him, for He is the cleft in which we shelter. Rock Etam teaches us to flee from every flawed savior to the true Rock of ages, cleft for us, in whose wounds the church finds a refuge that no Philistine and no death can storm.
webster_summary: The cleft rock where Samson dwelt after smiting the Philistines, whence Judah fetched him (Jdg 15:8, 11); a figure of the cleft rock of refuge and of the true Rock, Christ.

The rock could shelter his body but not mend his soul, and so it strains toward a greater Deliverer.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A cleft rock in Judah raises no modern quarrel. The principle to recover is that every flawed savior points beyond himself to the true Rock, the spiritual Rock that followed Israel, which was Christ. He is the hiding place from the wind, the shadow of a great rock in a weary land; flee from every lesser refuge to the Rock of ages, cleft for us.
